variants: Another standard on my frontier. I have counted your tents from the ridge - it did not take long. Rome has surveyed better men than you and buried them in straighter rows.
So this is the army. I make it three cohorts and some optimism. My clerks have already drawn up the receipt for your camp; we only need the date.
Keep the field, then. Rome does not lose provinces - she lends them, at interest. My accountants will be along in the spring, and they are far less pleasant than I am.
You have beaten a consul. Write it down somewhere; nobody in the city will believe you, and next year they will send two.
There. That is what happens when amateurs march against a ledger. Sit down. My men will count you when they have counted the horses.
You brought numbers. I brought arithmetic. Do write to your people and tell them the difference, if any of them can read.
Ah. Blades at last. I had begun to think you were a rumour with a baggage train.
The legion is moving. Do not trouble to form a line - it will only give my men something to step over.
I am sending the cohorts down now. Count them as they come. It will give you something to do with your last minutes.
Forward, in order. If you have a reserve, this would be the moment to discover it does not exist.
You are at my walls. Bold. My grandfather kept a dog that was bold; we buried it with honours and bought a better one.
Hitting my camp, are we? Every stone you knock loose has already been invoiced to your treasury.
You have that camp. Congratulations - you now own its wells, its debts, and its sanitation. I shall want it back before the rains.
One camp changes hands. I have lost more to a dishonest quartermaster and slept perfectly well.
That was yours a moment ago. My surveyors are already renaming the streets. Something Latin, I think.
Another camp for the Republic. Do stay and watch the standards go up; you will not see it done better.
Your line is thinning nicely. I am told grief is easier when one has fewer names to remember.
Look at them fall. I did warn you that arithmetic is cruel, and I am only its clerk.
My cohorts are bleeding. Very well. Rome bleeds the way rivers do - it is how she reaches the sea.
A fresh column is on the road to you. Treat them courteously; several of them owe me money.
Reinforcements march. Rome has a great many sons and a very short memory for their names.
Your commander is down. Pity. I had meant to invite him to dinner after and explain where he went wrong.
You have killed a consul. Rome keeps forty more in cupboards in the city, and I promise you the ones still in the cupboards are worse.
Nearly beaten, they tell me. I have been nearly beaten before. The word is doing a great deal of work in that sentence.
We fight together, then. Do try to keep your line straight - I shall be watching from the good ground, and I have a very long memory for embarrassments.
A victory, and a tidy one. I shall write it up as mostly mine; you would have done the same.
Beaten. Beside you, which stings. I shall mention that the ground was poor and the allies poorer.
My camp is under the hammer. If you have men to spare, spare them now; if not, I shall be curious to see what you were saving them for.
They are at my walls, and my walls were built by the lowest bidder. Some assistance would not go unrecorded.
I am losing cohorts faster than the treasury can replace them, and the treasury is quicker than you think.
This is what the end of a consulship looks like from the inside. Come quickly, or come for the funeral.
That is the end of my part. The rest of the war is yours. Do keep the receipts.
My cohorts are marching on them. Watch the manoeuvre; it is not something one sees twice for free.
I am attacking. If you wished to be consulted, you should have brought more men.
That camp is Rome's now. I shall let you have the wells, at the usual rate.
Your commander has fallen. Unfortunate. Hold your line; I shall not hold mine for a leaderless ally very long.
